analysis.one_liner: Adds a flat 38% deduction on capital gains, replacing a complex tiered rate schedule with a simple tax break for investors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the entire 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a flat 38% deduction for capital gains income, cutting the top effective tax rate on gains roughly in half, while keeping the alternative minimum tax from taking the deduction away. It also simplifies the tax code by consolidating a confusing set of special capital gains rates and rules — including repeal of a small-business stock exclusion, treatment of collectibles, and a repeal of a pending 2001 election — into a single deduction. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and saw no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals and families who realize large capital gains — investors, stockholders, and owners of appreciated assets — would pay sharply lower tax on those gains, with a simpler rule replacing the current confusing schedule of special rates.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a flat 38% deduction from gross income for any net capital gain, whether or not the taxpayer itemizes, cutting the effective top tax rate on gains roughly in half.
Replaces a patchwork of special capital gains rules — a small-business stock exclusion, a pending 2001 election, and collectibles special treatment — with one simpler deduction-based rule.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the lost revenue, and taxpayers who don't realize gains — primarily wage earners who owe tax at full rates — bear the tax code's growing tilt toward income from wealth; the government would have less money for spending or other tax cuts.

drawbacks.text: By excluding 38% of gains from tax, the bill would forgo substantial federal revenue that would otherwise come from taxpayers whose income comes from selling appreciated assets, shifting the tax burden toward wage income.
The deduction applies to all non-corporate taxpayers' net gains, so the largest dollar benefit flows to the biggest asset holders, who pay the top marginal rates on the remaining 62% of their gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a large, permanent tax cut concentrated on households with substantial appreciated assets while reducing federal revenue across the board. Its simplification benefits are real, but the overwhelming effect is a transfer to those with the largest investment income.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. William J. Coyne (D-PA) introduced the bill on April 14, 1999, with five original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 106th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's failure, but the federal Treasury retained revenue it would otherwise have lost, and the existing capital gains rate schedule — which already favored investment income — stayed in place unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and status quo taxpayers

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship (10 Democrats and 1 Republican among its 11 cosponsors) but never advanced far enough to generate recorded support or opposition.

industries.note: Would have paid roughly half the previous tax on large capital gains; the cost shows up as lost federal revenue and a larger relative tax burden on wage income.
The bill repeals a special exclusion for gains on small business stock, closing a tax preference in exchange for the broader flat deduction.
Would tax collectibles gains as short-term regardless of holding period, eliminating a preference for that asset class.
